11.text: HOUSE OF THE MARITIME CHUKCHEE. — The winter lodging of the

12.text: Maritime Chukchee is more or less similar to that of the Reindeer people.

13.text: The frame, however, is constructed differently, chiefly on account of the

14.text: scarcity of wood for poles. One great pole forms the central support (Plate XV,

15.text: Fig. 1). It is placed upright, its lower end being firmly stuck into the

16.text: ground, while the other end has a cross-piece tied to it to support the roof-

17.text: poles. Stakes of wood or of bone of the whale replace the vaˊrêt. They

18.text: are planted in the ground, and form the frame for the walls. The cross-

19.text: pieces and long poles are tied on as usual, but occasionally whales’ ribs are

20.text: used instead of wood. The whole structure is often surrounded by a low

21.text: wall of sod (Plate XV, Fig. 3) or of stones, and the cover drawn over the

22.text: frame is fastened to it by stones and pieces of sod. The stretchers with

23.text: cross-pieces are also used for tightening the cover. The entrance faces the

24.text: sea. It is often sheltered by a small structure of sod (Plate XVI, Fig. 1)

25.text: or of stones, or by a piece of tent-covering thrown over a few stakes, as in

26.text: the case of the winter houses of the Reindeer people.

27.text: For cutting the sod, digging the loose earth, and levelling the spot

28.text: intended for the house, shovels of wood and of walrus shoulder-blades (Fig.

29.text: 99, a, b), and picks of bone (Fig. 99, c), are used, though nowadays these are

30.text: gradually being superseded by iron implements. The forms of those made of

31.text: bone or wood are similar to those used by the American Eskimo.¹ Fig. 99, d,

32.text: represents a shovel collected among the Lamut, though the Kolyma Reindeer

33.text: Chukchee use exactly the same form. It also resembles the shovel used in

35.text: The covering of the house is for the most part sewed together out of worn-

36.text: out pieces of tent-covering bought from the Reindeer people. In front a large

37.text: walrus-skin is placed, in order to give protection against the storms, which

38.text: usually come from the sea. In more recent years old sail-cloth has begun to be

39.text: used instead of old reindeer-skins, especially in the Eskimo settlements. Every

40.text: part of the cover is well fastened with thongs, and weighted down by means

41.text: of heavy stones and loaded sledges, and even iron chains (Plate XV, Fig. 2).

42.text: The inner room is almost always double, both sections meeting at an angle.
